title: Medieval Najd
subtitle: 632–1517 · The Yamāma Province, the Ukhaydirid Emirate, the Bedouin Centuries and the Founding of the Oasis Towns

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: After the Ridda the plateau emptied and stayed poor — a Kharijite interlude, the two-century Ukhaydirid toll-state, the Qarmatian shadow, four centuries with no state at all, and then the 15th-century founding of the oasis towns

entries.group: The Yamāma Province and the Kharijite Interlude (632–750)
entries.label: Al-Yamāma emptied, governed from afar
entries.hint: After the Ridda, al-Yamāma was a province run from Basra and Bahrain, and its tribes — Tamīm, Bakr, Ḥanīfa — emigrated en masse to the garrison cities and the conquests. The plateau lost its people and its weight and became a backwater it would not leave for eight centuries.
entries.note: al-Tabari; al-Baladhuri, Futuḥ al-buldan; Donner, 'The Early Islamic Conquests' (1981).

entries.group: The Yamāma Province and the Kharijite Interlude (632–750)
entries.label: The Najdiyya Kharijites
entries.hint: Najda ibn ʿĀmir al-Ḥanafī led a Kharijite movement that briefly ruled al-Yamāma, al-Bahrain, ʿUmān and part of the Hijaz — the largest state the interior hosted between the Ridda and the Ukhaydirids. It fell apart in doctrinal schism within a decade.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the Kharijite heresiographies; Patricia Crone, 'The Nativist Prophets of Early Islamic Iran' (2012) for the wider context.

entries.label: The Ukhaydirid emirate
entries.hint: Ḥasanid sharifs, fleeing the Abbasid repression after the failed Kufa revolt of 865, seized al-Yamāma and ruled it for nearly two centuries — taxing the Hajj caravan and the oasis produce from a fortified capital. It is the last organised state in Najd before the Saudis.
entries.note: al-Hamdani, Ṣifat Jazīrat al-ʿArab; G. Rex Smith and others on the Ukhaydirids; the Saudi archaeological work on al-Kharj.

entries.label: Nāṣir-i Khusraw's Yamāma
entries.hint: The Persian traveller passed through and left a rare eyewitness account: a fortified oasis-state under a feared Alid amir with a personal army, its people poor and taxed, its water carefully controlled — the Ukhaydirid emirate near its end.
entries.note: Nāṣir-i Khusraw, Safarnāma, on his crossing of Arabia in 1050.

entries.label: The Qarmatians reach across the plateau
entries.hint: The Ismaili Qarmatian state of al-Aḥsāʾ raided the Hajj caravans across Najd, carried off the Black Stone from Mecca in 930, and for a century dominated the routes. Every Najd tribe and town had to reckon with it, and few could resist it.
entries.note: al-Tabari; Ibn al-Athir; Wilferd Madelung, 'The Fatimids and the Qarmatis of Bahrain'.

entries.label: The bedouin centuries
entries.hint: After the Ukhaydirids, no state held Najd for nearly four hundred years. The plateau belonged to its confederations — ʿAnaza, Ṭayyiʾ and then Shammar, Banū Lām, the Daʿāsir — and to its oasis amīrs, who paid the strongest tribe a fixed tribute to be left alone.
entries.note: the later Najdi chronicle tradition compiling earlier material; Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd, on the pre-Saudi tribal order.

entries.group: The Amīr al-ʿArab and the Mamluk Shadow (c.1260–1450)
entries.label: The Āl Faḍl and the 'commander of the Arabs'
entries.loc: the northern Najd and the Syrian desert
entries.hint: The Mamluks of Egypt appointed the chief of the Āl Faḍl of the Syrian steppe as amīr al-ʿarab, with a nominal claim over the northern Najd tribes and the Hajj road — an outside power's cheapest way of pretending to govern the interior.
entries.note: al-Qalqashandi, Ṣubḥ al-aʿshā, on the amīr al-ʿarab; Mustafa Hiyari, 'The origins and development of the Amīrate of the Arabs' (1975).

entries.group: The Jabrids and the New Oasis Towns (c.1450–1517)
entries.label: The Jabrids
entries.hint: The Banū Jabr, a Sunni bedouin dynasty out of al-Aḥsāʾ, at their height under Ajwad ibn Zāmil held al-Aḥsāʾ, al-Qaṭīf and a wide stretch of Najd, and raided into ʿUmān — the nearest thing to a Najd-spanning power in the late medieval centuries.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the Portuguese and Ottoman accounts of eastern Arabia; the Jabrid coinage.

entries.group: The Jabrids and the New Oasis Towns (c.1450–1517)
entries.label: The new oasis towns
entries.loc: Wadi Ḥanīfa, al-Qaṣīm and Jabal Shammar
entries.hint: Through the 15th century the settled Najd of the Saudi era took shape: al-ʿUyayna and al-Dirʿiyya in Wadi Ḥanīfa — Dirʿiyya founded around 1446 by Māniʿ al-Muraydī, ancestor of the Āl Saʿūd — Buraydah and ʿUnayzah in al-Qaṣīm, and Ḥāʾil under Jabal Shammar.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd; the Dirʿiyya foundation tradition; the Saudi historical atlases.

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The Kharijite wars, the Qarmatian raids on the pilgrimage, the permanent low war of the raid and the tribute, the great tribal migrations, and the Jabrid campaigns

entries.label: The rise and fall of the Najdiyya
entries.hint: Najda's movement spread across eastern and central Arabia at speed and then destroyed itself — deposing Najda over a point of doctrine, splitting into rival factions, and being finished off by the Umayyads and by other Kharijites.
entries.note: al-Tabari; the Kharijite subsect literature.

entries.label: The raids on the Hajj
entries.loc: the Hajj road across Najd, and Mecca
entries.hint: The Qarmatians repeatedly fell on the pilgrim caravans crossing the plateau, and in 930 they sacked Mecca itself and took the Black Stone. For a generation the interior route was too dangerous to use, and the Hajj sometimes did not go at all.
entries.note: Ibn al-Athir; al-Masʿudi; Madelung on the Qarmati raids.

entries.label: The khuwa and the ghazw
entries.hint: The plateau's permanent condition: the bedouin raid (ghazw) for camels and standing, the protection tribute (khuwa) the towns and weaker tribes paid the strong, and the feud that ran between them. It was low-level, chronic, and structural.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the ethnographic literature on Najdi raiding (Dickson, Musil); Hoyland (2001) for the deep background.

entries.label: The tribal migrations
entries.hint: The great 11th-century movement of the Banū Hilāl and Banū Sulaym out of the Najd–Hijaz borderland toward Egypt and North Africa, and the southward and eastward push of Shammar, ʿAnaza and Ṭayyiʾ, redrew the tribal map of the interior.
entries.note: Ibn Khaldun on the Hilālī migration; the modern tribal geographies (Oppenheim, 'Die Beduinen').

entries.label: The Jabrid campaigns and collapse
entries.hint: Ajwad ibn Zāmil fought to hold al-Aḥsāʾ, dominate Najd and raid ʿUmān; after his death the dynasty fell apart under Portuguese pressure on the Gulf and the rise of the Banū Khālid, who took al-Aḥsāʾ within a generation.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the Portuguese Gulf chronicles; the Banū Khālid takeover c.1670 completes the process later.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: The Ukhaydirid toll-state, the one piece of infrastructure an empire ever built here, and the two homegrown institutions of a stateless land — the khuwa contract and the town amirate

entries.label: The Ukhaydirid toll-state
entries.hint: The Ukhaydirid amīrs governed by taxing movement — the Hajj caravan, the trade, the oasis produce — from a fortified capital, with a reputation for harshness. It was a rare instance of Najdi statehood, and the sources remember it as an unloved one.
entries.note: Nāṣir-i Khusraw, Safarnāma; al-Hamdani on the Yamāma under the sharifs.

entries.label: The Darb Zubayda road service
entries.loc: the Kufa–Mecca road across the northern plateau
entries.hint: The Abbasid state built and maintained the Kufa–Mecca pilgrim road across the northern plateau — wells, stone reservoirs, milestones, forts, staging posts and a road patrol. It is the one thing an empire ever built and ran inside Najd.
entries.note: Saʿad al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah: The Pilgrim Road from Kufa to Mecca' (1980); the Saudi Antiquities surveys.

entries.label: The khuwa system as the plateau's order
entries.hint: With no state, security was a contract: an oasis town or a weak tribe paid a strong tribe a fixed annual tribute (khuwa), and the strong tribe then guaranteed its safety and escorted its caravans. It was a recognised institution with its own rules and its own breaches.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr; the ethnographic accounts (Musil, 'The Manners and Customs of the Rwala Bedouins', 1928); Landau-Tasseron on protection in Arabian society.

entries.label: The town amirate
entries.hint: Each oasis town was governed by an amīr, usually from a leading settled family, who held the fort, judged disputes, organised the date harvest and the defence, and negotiated the khuwa. It is the political building block the Saudi state would later assemble into a country.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd; Uwaidah al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: A Kharijite plateau that turned solidly Sunni and then Ḥanbalī, the scholarly town of Ushayqir, the shrine-and-tree religion of the oases, and a Sufi presence — the last two being what the reform movement would target

entries.label: Kharijism and its disappearance
entries.hint: The early plateau had a strong Kharijite and Ibadi current — the Najdiyya were its high point. After that movement's fall it faded fast, and by the high medieval period Najd was solidly Sunni: one of the sharpest sectarian reversals in Islamic history.
entries.note: the Kharijite heresiographies; al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002).

entries.label: Najd becomes a Ḥanbalī land
entries.hint: From the later medieval centuries the settled towns adopted the Ḥanbalī school, the strictest of the Sunni four, and Najdi students went to Damascus, Cairo and Medina to study it — the network that carried the ideas of Ibn Taymiyya back to the plateau.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); George Makdisi on the Ḥanbalī tradition; the biographical dictionaries of Najdi ʿulamāʾ.

entries.label: Ushayqir, the town of the ʿulamāʾ
entries.hint: The small oasis of Ushayqir became Najd's main centre of learning, home to the scholarly families — including the teachers of the Āl al-Shaykh — who kept a manuscript and teaching tradition alive in a land with almost no cities and no libraries.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); ʿAbd Allah al-Bassam, 'ʿUlamaʾ Najd khilal thamaniyat qurun'.

entries.label: The shrine, the tree and the stone
entries.hint: Popular practice across Najd centred on tombs, trees, caves and stones — the shrine of Zayd ibn al-Khaṭṭāb at al-Jubayla, the 'male palm' of Dhū Saʿab, the tomb of Ḍirār, the sacred cave. This is the everyday religion that Muḥammad ibn ʿAbd al-Wahhāb would set out to destroy.
entries.note: Ibn Ghannam, Rawḍat al-afkar (a hostile Wahhābī source, listing the sites the movement targeted); al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: Sufism on the plateau
entries.loc: the oasis towns and the Hajj road
entries.hint: Sufi orders and wandering shaykhs had a presence in the Najdi towns and along the pilgrim road — teaching, healing, mediating feud — tolerated and at times influential, and part of the religious landscape the reform movement reacted against.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); the biographical notices of Sufi figures in the Najdi scholarly dictionaries.

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: The engineered landscape of the Hajj road, the mud-brick Najdi town in its classic form, the birth of vernacular Nabaṭī poetry, the Hilālī epic, and the samir and the ʿarda

entries.label: The Darb Zubayda as engineered landscape
entries.loc: the northern plateau, Faid and the road stations
entries.hint: The round and rectangular stone reservoirs (birak), the paved cuts through rock, the milestones and the fort at Faid are the largest man-made structures of medieval Najd and among the best-preserved early Islamic infrastructure anywhere in the world.
entries.note: al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah' (1980); the 2015 Saudi UNESCO tentative listing and later inscription of the pilgrimage routes.

entries.label: The Najdi mud-brick town
entries.loc: Wadi Ḥanīfa and al-Qaṣīm, Saudi Arabia
entries.hint: The classic Najdi form settled in this period: the palm-log-roofed courtyard house, the fortified qaṣr, the mosque with its stubby stepped minaret, the town wall and its round watchtowers — all built in unfired earth, refined over centuries into something hard to storm.
entries.note: the surviving earthen architecture of al-Dirʿiyya (at-Turaif), Ushayqir and old ʿUnayzah; Geoffrey King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998).

entries.label: Nabaṭī poetry
entries.hint: The vernacular poetry of Arabia — composed in the spoken dialect rather than classical Arabic, but keeping the old desert themes and much of the old form — emerges as a distinct, named tradition in these centuries. Its early figures are half-legendary; the form is fully alive by 1500.
entries.note: Saad Sowayan, 'Nabaṭi Poetry: The Oral Poetry of Arabia' (1985); Marcel Kurpershoek, 'Oral Poetry and Narratives from Central Arabia'.

entries.label: Sīrat Banī Hilāl
entries.loc: the Najd–Hijaz borderland, then Egypt and the Maghreb
entries.hint: The folk epic of the Banū Hilāl's wanderings and their conquest of the west took its Arabian core in the Najd–Hijaz margins and then travelled — with the migration itself — across Egypt into Ifrīqiya, where it is still performed.
entries.note: Bridget Connelly, 'Arab Folk Epic and Identity' (1986); Susan Slyomovics, 'The Merchant of Art' (1987).

entries.label: The samir and the ʿarda
entries.loc: the oasis towns and the tribal camps
entries.hint: The samir — the night gathering with its sung poetry and hand-clapping — and the ʿarda — the war-dance of men in ranks with drums, raised swords and a chanted poem — are the performance culture of settled and nomadic Najd alike, and both survive today.
entries.note: Sowayan on the samir; Lisa Urkevich, 'Music and Traditions of the Arabian Peninsula' (2015).

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: Al-Hamdani's detailed account of the interior, the Najdi scholarly network that linked a stateless land to the wider Sunni world, and the modern archaeology now recovering the medieval plateau

entries.label: Al-Hamdani's Yamāma
entries.hint: The 10th-century geographer's Ṣifat Jazīrat al-ʿArab describes the towns, wells, tribes and routes of Najd in detail, and his Kitāb al-Jawharatayn treats its gold and silver. It is the fullest medieval account of the interior by a very wide margin.
entries.note: al-Hamdani, Ṣifat Jazīrat al-ʿArab (ed. Müller) and Kitāb al-Jawharatayn al-ʿatīqatayn.

entries.label: The Najdi scholarly network
entries.hint: From a handful of oasis towns, Najdi ʿulamāʾ built links to the wider Sunni world through study travel and correspondence — importing books, law and ideas, and keeping a literate tradition alive in a place with no cities, no courts and no patrons.
entries.note: al-Bassam, 'ʿUlamaʾ Najd'; al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002).

entries.label: Recovering medieval Najd
entries.loc: the Darb Zubayda, Faid and al-Kharj
entries.hint: Saudi archaeology — the surveys of the Darb Zubayda and Faid, the excavations at al-Yamāma and the Ukhaydirid sites — has begun to give the interior's medieval centuries a material record to set against the thin and scattered texts.
entries.note: al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah' (1980); the al-Yamāma archaeological project (Riyadh / CNRS).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: The northern plateau lived off the pilgrimage, the oasis towns off the date palm, and the tribes off their herds and the ʿasīl horse they bred and sold

entries.label: The Hajj and the caravan economy
entries.loc: the Darb Zubayda and Faid, northern Najd
entries.hint: The northern plateau lived off the pilgrimage — provisioning the caravans, guiding and guarding them, selling them water, fodder and dates. Faid and the road stations rose with the traffic and shrank when war or the Qarmatians closed the route.
entries.note: al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah' (1980); the economic history of the Hajj (Peters, 'The Hajj', 1994).

entries.label: The oasis date economy
entries.hint: The settled towns ran on the date palm, irrigated from deep wells by camel-drawn bucket. The crop fed the town, paid the khuwa, and was traded to the bedouin for meat, wool, ghee and transport — the axis of settled–nomad exchange.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); Varisco and the wider literature on Arabian oasis agriculture.

entries.label: The horse trade
entries.loc: Najd · exported through the Gulf and to Syria and Egypt
entries.hint: The Najd tribes bred the ʿasīl Arabian horse and sold it, at very high prices, to Egypt, Syria and — through the Gulf ports — to India. It was the plateau's one luxury export and a real source of tribal wealth and prestige.
entries.note: the medieval and early modern accounts of the Arabian horse trade; the Mamluk demand for Najdi horses documented in al-Qalqashandi.

entries.label: The pastoral surplus
entries.hint: The bedouin economy of camel and small-stock herding, and the exchange with the oases — animals, wool, ghee and transport labour for dates, grain, cloth and weapons. Neither half could live without the other, and both said they could.
entries.note: the ethnographic literature (Musil, Dickson); al-Juhany (2002) on settled–nomad exchange.

entries.label: Mines and salt
entries.hint: The gold and silver workings al-Hamdani lists, the salt flats worked for the caravan and oasis trade, and minor stone and metal extraction supplemented a thin economy. None of it amounted to more than a local supplement.
entries.note: al-Hamdani, Kitāb al-Jawharatayn; the Saudi geological surveys of ancient mining.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The well and the animal-drawn bucket that made every oasis, the state-scale reservoirs of the Hajj road, and a fortification tradition in cheap earth

entries.label: Well and saniya irrigation
entries.hint: The deep hand-dug well, a leather bucket on a pulley hauled up by a camel or donkey walking a ramp (the saniya or gharrāf), and mud-lined channels to the palm plots — the water technology that made a Najdi oasis town possible, and limited how big it could grow.
entries.note: King, 'The Traditional Architecture of Saudi Arabia' (1998); the ethnographic descriptions of Najdi irrigation.

entries.label: The reservoirs of the Hajj road
entries.hint: The Darb Zubayda's stone-built birak — some over sixty metres across, plastered watertight, fed by walled catchment channels — were a state-scale water technology dropped into the open desert for the single purpose of keeping the pilgrimage alive.
entries.note: al-Rashid, 'Darb Zubaydah' (1980); the surviving birak at al-Rabadha, Faid and along the route.

entries.label: Earthen fortification
entries.hint: The mud-brick town wall, the round corner tower, the fortified palace and the mosque-fort — a defensive architecture in the cheapest possible material, thickened and battered and loopholed over generations into something a raiding party could not take.
entries.note: King (1998); the surviving defensive architecture of at-Turaif in Dirʿiyya.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: A plateau the Caliphate used and ignored, the Qarmatian regional hegemony, the Hilālī migration carrying Najd's culture west, the study travel that brought Ibn Taymiyya's ideas home, and the move that put the Āl Saʿūd in Wadi Ḥanīfa

entries.label: Najd and the Caliphate
entries.loc: the plateau · and Damascus and Baghdad
entries.hint: Najd gave the conquests their fighters and was then left almost entirely alone. The Umayyads, the Abbasids and their successors governed at most the Hajj road across the north and never troubled with the interior — there was nothing there worth the cost.
entries.note: al-Baladhuri; al-Juhany (2002) on Najd's marginality.

entries.label: The Qarmatian shadow
entries.hint: For a century and a half the Ismaili state of al-Aḥsāʾ was the dominant regional power, its raids and its grip on the trade routes forcing every Najd tribe and town into some accommodation with it — tribute, alliance or flight.
entries.note: Madelung, 'The Fatimids and the Qarmatis of Bahrain'; Ibn al-Athir.

entries.label: The Banū Hilāl migration
entries.loc: the Najd–Hijaz margins · to Egypt and the Maghreb
entries.hint: The westward movement of the Banū Hilāl and Banū Sulaym, encouraged by the Fatimids, carried Najdi and Hijazi tribes across Egypt into Ifrīqiya and the Maghreb — and carried their dialect, their poetry and their epic with them.
entries.note: Ibn Khaldun, Kitāb al-ʿIbar, on the Hilālī migration and its cultural effects.

entries.label: Study abroad and the return of a book
entries.loc: Damascus, Cairo, Medina · and back to Najd
entries.hint: Najdi scholars travelled to the Sunni centres to study and came home with law, method and books — the channel through which Ḥanbalī jurisprudence and, above all, the works of Ibn Taymiyya reached the plateau and were copied and taught there.
entries.note: al-Bassam, 'ʿUlamaʾ Najd'; Michael Cook, 'On the Origins of Wahhābism' (1992).

entries.label: Dirʿiyya's founding move
entries.hint: Māniʿ al-Muraydī brought his people west from the al-Qaṭīf district, at the invitation of a relative who was amīr of Ḥajr, and settled two stretches of Wadi Ḥanīfa. The migration put the ancestors of the Āl Saʿūd exactly where they would need to be three centuries later.
entries.note: Ibn Bishr, ʿUnwan al-majd; the Dirʿiyya foundation narrative.

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: Eight centuries of poverty and statelessness with a road running through, a whole region changing its sect, and a 15th-century turn as the oasis towns and the scholarly network take root

entries.label: The long marginality of Najd
entries.hint: For eight centuries the interior was a poor, stateless, half-forgotten land — no city, no dynasty of consequence, no reason for any empire to conquer it. Its recorded history in this period is largely the history of the pilgrim road crossing its northern edge.
entries.note: al-Juhany, 'Najd before the Salafi Reform Movement' (2002); Madawi Al-Rasheed, 'A History of Saudi Arabia' (2010), on the deep background.

entries.label: The sectarian re-alignment
entries.hint: Najd went from a Kharijite and Ibadi stronghold in the 7th century to a Sunni and increasingly Ḥanbalī land by the 15th — one of the clearest cases anywhere of a whole region changing its religious identity over the medieval centuries.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); the Kharijite and Ḥanbalī biographical literatures.

entries.label: The oasis towns coalesce
entries.loc: Wadi Ḥanīfa, al-Qaṣīm and Jabal Shammar
entries.hint: The 15th century is the turning point: new walled towns founded, tribal chieftaincies settling into hereditary town amirates, the Ḥanbalī scholarly network putting down roots. The Najd that the Saudi state would one day unite is assembling itself.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); the Najdi town foundation traditions in Ibn Bishr.

entries.label: The thread continues — al-ʿUyayna, Dirʿiyya and the pact of 1744
entries.hint: The folio ends where oasis-town Najd is fully formed and its scholarly tradition established. Within two and a half centuries a scholar of al-ʿUyayna and the amīr of Dirʿiyya will make the alliance that creates the first Saudi state — the subject of the next two folios.
entries.note: a forward reference: najd-1517-1744 and najd-1744-1900 are planned but not yet built.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: Women in the oasis and the camp, the enslaved Africans of the towns, the protected non-tribal Ṣulubba, and the deep divide and constant traffic between nomad and townsman

entries.label: Women in the oasis and the camp
entries.hint: The settled woman ran the household economy and worked the harvest under close constraint; the bedouin woman had more mobility and a recognised public voice in the camp. The poetry preserves women's laments and satires where the chronicles record nothing at all.
entries.note: Sowayan on women's Nabaṭī poetry; Moshe Piamenta and the ethnographic accounts of Najdi women's lives.

entries.label: Enslaved Africans in Najd
entries.loc: the oasis towns and the tribes
entries.hint: The Red Sea and Gulf slave trades brought enslaved people into the oasis towns as farm and domestic labour and into the tribes as herders and fighters. A small but permanent enslaved and freed population — the khadam — formed in every Najdi town.
entries.note: the general literature on slavery in Arabia (Clarence-Smith, 'Islam and the Abolition of Slavery', 2006); the Najdi town social structure in al-Juhany (2002).

entries.label: The Ṣulubba
entries.hint: A non-tribal people of the northern desert — tinkers, hunters, guides and musicians — moving freely among the tribes under a kind of universal protection, holding no territory and no camels, and telling, or having told about them, many contradictory stories of their origin.
entries.note: Alois Musil and Werner Caskel on the Ṣulubba; the enduring uncertainty about their history.

entries.label: The badū and the ḥaḍar
entries.hint: The divide between the nomad and the townsman — economically interdependent, socially wary, each holding the other slightly beneath him — is the organising fact of Najdi society and the frame of every later account of it, foreign and local alike.
entries.note: al-Juhany (2002); Ibn Khaldun's ʿumrān badawī / ʿumrān ḥaḍarī distinction as the classic statement.
